summary: This Wikipedia-derived note traces the dissolution of the Soviet Union through 1985-1991 events, including Gorbachev's reforms, the 1989 Congress of People's Deputies elections, and nationalist movements in Ukraine, Moldova, Lithuania and Kazakhstan. It covers the Warsaw Pact revolutions of 1989, the failed August 1991 coup, and the Belavezha Accords of December 1991 that created the CIS. It ends with the flag lowering on December 25, 1991 and the Soviet Union's formal end on December 26, 1991.
one_line: Chronicles the 1985-1991 reforms, nationalist movements and 1991 Belavezha Accords that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union.
key_facts: In spring 1989 the Soviet Union held limited democratic elections to the Congress of People's Deputies, the first since 1917, with uncensored live TV coverage of its deliberations.
The 1989 Polish limited experiment with democracy quickly led to the toppling of the Communist government in Warsaw that summer.
On December 8, 1991, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus signed the Belavezha Accords in Belavezhskaya Pushcha, western Belarus, proclaiming the Soviet Union had ceased to exist.
The Belavezha Accords announced formation of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) as a looser association to replace the Soviet Union.
The Jeltoqsan riots in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan began on December 17, 1986, after Gorbachev replaced Dinmukhamed Konayev with Gennady Kolbin, an outsider from the Russian SFSR.
On December 7, 1989, the Communist Party of Lithuania under Algirdas Brazauskas split from the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
On April 6, 1990, the Lviv City Council voted to return St. George Cathedral to the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.
On June 5-6, 1990, Metropolitan Mstyslav was elected patriarch of the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church during that Church's first synod.
Beginning in February 1988, the Democratic Movement of Moldova organized public meetings, demonstrations, and song festivals in Chişinău.
In May 1985 Gorbachev delivered a speech in Leningrad advocating reforms and an anti-alcohol campaign, raising prices on vodka, wine, and beer.
The Russian Supreme Soviet ratified the Belavezha Accords and renounced the 1922 Union Treaty on December 12, 1991.
Gorbachev abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine in favor of non-intervention, jokingly termed the Sinatra Doctrine after the Frank Sinatra song 'My Way'.
On the night of December 25, 1991, at 7:32 p.m. Moscow time, the Soviet flag was lowered for the last time and the Russian tricolor was raised.
On December 26, 1991, the Council of Republics issued a formal Declaration recognizing the Soviet Union had ceased to exist as a state and subject of international law.

entities.name: Congress of People's Deputies
entities.role: new central legislature whose 1989 limited competitive elections were held, with live TV coverage of its deliberations

entities.name: Gorbachev
entities.role: Soviet leader who sought to restructure the Soviet Union, reform communism, and abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine

entities.name: Dinmukhamed Konayev
entities.role: First Secretary of the Communist Party of Kazakhstan, an ethnic Kazakh dismissed by Gorbachev in December 1986

entities.name: Gennady Kolbin
entities.role: outsider from the Russian SFSR who replaced Konayev as First Secretary in Kazakhstan

entities.name: Volodymyr Ivashko
entities.role: leader of the Communist Party of Ukraine (CPU) elected parliament chair on June 4, 1990 with 60 percent of the vote

entities.name: Mstyslav
entities.role: Metropolitan of the U.S.-based Ukrainian Orthodox Church, elected patriarch of the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church in June 1990

entities.name: Yeltsin
entities.role: Russian Federation leader whose office was in the White House, who rallied opposition to the coup atop a tank

entities.name: Kravchuk
entities.role: chairman of the Ukrainian parliament who signed a 10-year bilateral pact with Yeltsin on November 19, 1990

entities.name: Algirdas Brazauskas
entities.role: leader of the Communist Party of Lithuania that split from the CPSU on December 7, 1989

entities.name: Mykolas Burokevičius
entities.role: hardliner who headed a smaller loyalist Communist Party faction in Lithuania affiliated with the CPSU

entities.name: Vytautas Landsbergis
entities.role: first non-Communist president of Lithuania since its forced incorporation into the USSR

entities.name: Alexander Yakovlev
entities.role: official who noted annual collections of alcohol taxes decreased by 100 billion rubles

entities.name: Anatol Şalaru
entities.role: submitted a proposal on January 15, 1988 to continue the Moldovan movement's meetings at the Mihai Eminescu bust

entities.name: Volodymyr Scherbytsky
entities.role: first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, lampooned as 'the mastodon of stagnation'

entities.name: Cardinal Myroslav Lubachivsky
entities.role: proclaimed a day of prayer and fasting on November 26, 1989

entities.name: Democratic Movement of Moldova
entities.role: movement that organized public meetings, demonstrations and song festivals from February 1988 calling for national awakening

entities.name: Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church
entities.role: church that declared full independence from the Moscow Patriarchate in June 1990

entities.name: Ukrainian Helsinki Union
entities.role: disbanded on April 29-30, 1990 to form the Ukrainian Republican Party

entities.name: Belavezha Accords
entities.role: December 1991 agreement proclaiming the Soviet Union had ceased to exist and forming the CIS

entities.role: looser association announced in the Belavezha Accords to take the Soviet Union's place

entities.role: jokingly termed name for Gorbachev's policy of non-intervention in allies' internal affairs
